## Decision record: live Jev inference is authorized (2026-10-06)

The repository owner supplied a TypeSafe API key during the build and answered two questions from the orchestrator. This supersedes rules 3 and 4 of `orchestration/PROMPT.md` where they say no live call will be made.

- **Authorized:** live calls to Jev for this build.
- **Spending limit:** **$25 total** for the whole build. The orchestrator converts this to request/token caps from TypeSafe's published pricing, enforces them through the #64 budget guard, keeps a running ledger in progress comments here, and stops to ask before exceeding it.
- **Scope:** **record real fixtures.** Once the live backend (#64) is merged, each recipe is run against the real model and its responses are committed as `recorded` fixtures with the model string the API returned and the date. Notebooks still run offline by default, replaying those fixtures.

What does not change:

- No live call happens before #64 is merged and Opus-approved. Until then everything is offline and `synthetic`.
- `recorded` is still only for answers captured from a real API call. Nothing is hand-written and labelled recorded.
- Any number in a notebook or README is reported as measured on N examples with the model version, per section 2 of the recipe contract. No general claim about Jev's quality, latency, or cost.
- The key lives in an untracked, git-ignored file outside every agent worktree. It never appears in a commit, a notebook output, a log, a pull request, or an issue. Reviewers check this on every pull request.
- CI stays offline and keyless.

Ledger: $0.00 spent so far.

**Cumulative live spend: $0.0000118 of $25.00.** Requests made: 1. No reservations.

### Why this one took two reviewers and six fix rounds

**The decision:** this recipe deliberately ships with **no confidence gate**, where all 32 other published recipes and the template have one. That required two independent approvals under the same standard applied to changes to the template and the scaffolder, because the 27 recipes still to be built inherit the precedent.

**The grounds, as measured rather than argued:** `select_confidence_threshold` on this rule's own auto-selected validation pool returns **0.19**, the lowest observed confidence, and a gate there sends **0 of 20** validation and **0 of 20** test tasks to review. A house-conforming gate here is therefore a **dead branch**, which the recipe's own independence tests reject. The choice was never two branches or three — it was two consequential branches against two plus a dead one.

**And the ordering question dissolved on a contract reading rather than a trade-off.** `docs/glossary.md`'s rule is conditional — it governs the reason string *for a confidence-gated review* — so a recipe without such a review breaches nothing in the lexicon, while the guard enforcing it is unconditional. That is the check's defect, tracked separately, and a recipe pull request may not touch the guard or the allowlist. There was nothing to sequence.

**Four successive justifications for that decision were each wrong in a different way**: algebraic and false at the frozen threshold; measured but wrong in three particulars; an inverted inference about which threshold the house objective would pick (a review note, never shipped); and a claim **true of the original fixture pool** and falsified by the round that expanded it. Every one was caught by asking a reviewer to **verify a derivation at the current numbers** rather than read it. The surviving argument is printed, test-pinned, or both — and `test_perfect_validation_accuracy_is_infeasible_on_the_margin_pool` asserts the structural cause *and* the `ValueError`, so a fixture edit that made a perfect threshold reachable fails a test instead of quietly staling a comment.

**The recipe's code and fixtures were sound throughout.** Every one of those failures was in prose or a comment explaining the code.

### The best thing either review produced, now house guidance

Deleting this recipe's business cutoff **raises** coverage **and** accuracy on both splits with **no new error** — which looks like a branch earning nothing. It is not. The pick the cutoff holds back is the **argmax of gold among what was retrieved** — gold level 1, `related`, which the rubric's own words call *not suitable* — so top-1 scores naming it as **correct**.

**An argmax-against-gold metric is structurally blind to "the best candidate is still inadequate", and a fixed business cutoff is what covers it.** Top-1 only asks whether the best of a set was named; it cannot ask whether the set held anything worth acting on. So a quality floor shows up as **coverage**, not as accuracy or risk — and a test asserting only "risk rises" would fail to detect a floor doing real work. That is why this recipe's branch test asserts coverage *and* accuracy. Recorded in the house brief at the finding reviewer's request, since it generalises to every recipe whose headline metric is an argmax.

## Recipe 45 (Memory reconciliation) merged — #268 as `335e2e3`. **45 of 60 published; 30 merges**

### What the recipe does

A four-way `Choice` — `corroborating`, `superseding`, `contradicting`, `unrelated` — over a new memory statement against existing evidence. It uses the shared `jev_cookbook.simulation.Store` rather than reimplementing one, and `helpers.reconcile` is the policy layer above it: a below-gate answer goes to the review queue and **writes nothing**; `unrelated` writes nothing as a *complete* answer rather than a deferral; `corroborating` and `superseding` write while leaving the superseded value in history; and `contradicting` **never overwrites the live value**, writing the contested statement under a conflict key with a `ConflictRecord` so both sides stay reachable. The thing `Store` lacks — a notion of two writes disagreeing — is built in the recipe, and both the builder and the reviewer looked for a shared-code gap and agreed there was none.

### The finding that mattered, and the rule it produced

The recipe originally reported two zero-request baselines at 0.2500 against its own 0.9375, a headline gap of `+0.6875`. Its scored splits are built **exactly four per outcome**, and on a pool balanced *k* ways **every constant-prediction baseline scores exactly 1/k by arithmetic alone** — the majority class is undefined, the two baselines are identical to each other for the same structural reason, and the test offered as the guard against a dominated headline could not fail for any mechanism above chance.

Nothing printed was false and the balance was disclosed in the prose, so this was not a falsehood; it was **baseline selection**, which the existing rule about dominated headlines did not address. The reviewer sharpened the diagnosis past the orchestrator's: the test is not literally unable to fail — it fires when the mechanism is at or below chance, and any class imbalance fires an earlier assertion instead — so the accurate statement is that **there is no state in which the dominated-headline property is both at risk and checked**. That makes "it is checked rather than assumed" an overclaim rather than a falsehood.

The reviewer then settled whether a real baseline was even available **by building one**: keyword cues plus token overlap, zero requests, about ten minutes.

It took the better resolution rather than the cheaper one. The constant baselines are now labelled as **one structural floor reported twice, not two independent comparisons**, with the four-per-outcome structure itself **pinned by a new test** so the arithmetic argument is a checked property of the fixtures rather than a prose claim. And it added a non-constant, zero-request `keyword_overlap_baseline` that earns its accuracy from the statements' own text, so it could in principle tie or beat the mechanism.

Honest result: **0.8125 against 0.9375 — a two-row margin on sixteen rows**, printed as `+0.1250 accuracy, for 16 more requests`, where the cell previously claimed `+0.6875`. The thin number is the **correct outcome** of the finding, not a regression.

And the README now states what is proven **and names the failure mode it avoided**, so the recipe teaches the finding rather than merely dropping a false claim.

The general lesson: *"300 cases passed"* is not a reassuring silence but a reassuring **number**. The question is not "could this instrument report a difference" — a fuzz reports differences constantly, on inputs that do not matter — but **"of the inputs this fuzz generated, how many reached the branch I am claiming to have tested?"** A randomised test's input distribution is part of the test, and an unmeasured input distribution is an untested one.

## Foundation: the objective-pin guard is live — #273 merged as `d99d369`. **#244 items 1 and 4 delivered**

All 56 CI legs green on the integrated head, 30 post-merge legs green on `main`. Three fix rounds, four reviews. #244 stays **open** for item 3.

### What landed

A fail-closed check requiring that, for every real `select_confidence_threshold(` / `select_threshold(` call a recipe's committed notebook or `helpers.py` actually makes — found by walking real `ast.Call` nodes, never a text scan a decorative print can fool — the objective keyword be asserted in that recipe's tests **against a value traced to a read of the real committed source**, at **operand level**, with polarity tracked through an enclosing `not`. Plus a working pin in the template, so a builder following it gets a real one for free, and a documented generalisation of the allowlist's issue-naming protocol.

**31 recipes remain allowlisted** as genuinely unpinned (01–27 except 28, plus 29, 30, 33, 35); **16 pass un-allowlisted** (28, 31, 32, 34, 36–46 and `_template`). That list is item 3's work. Each reason ends `see #244`, and `strict=True` makes a fix that forgets to remove its entry a hard failure, so the allowlist cannot go stale in either direction.

### Why it took three rounds, which is the part worth keeping

The defect this check exists to fix is **a check keyed on a source idiom certifying the letter of a rule it cannot observe.** The check became that defect twice before it stopped being it.

**Round 1** recognised one spelling of the evidence and therefore **refused four recipes that had real pins** — 28, 41, 42 and 44 — proved by mutation, not argued. One of them parses the real call's AST and asserts the bound keyword's value, which is *stronger* than the idiom the check demanded. The allowlist asserted something **false** about those four, with the correction sitting in a PR body that dangles after a squash merge.

**Round 2** traced the tie at **statement** level, so an assert was credited whenever a tainted name and a spelling merely appeared in the same statement. That admitted a tautology, a `not(x in y)` polarity inversion, and an extraction route whose operand did no work — three spellings of one defect.

**Round 3** moved the tie to **operand** level. That is the version on `main`.

Two readings had to be withdrawn along the way. The first was this issue's own framing, that recipes were not pinning the objective. The second was mine: I reported the round-1 output as "35 of 45 recipes do not pin it, so the briefing did not transfer" and drew a lesson about builders ignoring guidance. **Both halves were wrong.** The genuine count is about 32, and what actually happened is that **46 hand-written pins drift into five different shapes** — which is what compliance across many independent authors looks like. The engineering problem was never mechanising a rule; it was **recognising a property under variation.** A count produced by the instrument under review is not independent of it.

### A defect found in the process of fixing it

A recipe's pin can be **poisoned by its own mutation proof**. This project requires a pin to be proved by mutation — show inside the pin test that changing the pinned thing makes the assertion fail. One recipe's test therefore contains the literal `"target_accuracy=1.0"`, harvested from its own proof line. A presence-matching check reads that counterexample as the claim, and a real keyword swap on that recipe went undetected.

The recipe does exactly what the contract asks, and that good behaviour creates the string that defeats the check. The operand-level fix resolves it by construction, because a constructed-mutation literal is never *compared against* a value read from the artefact. Verified against the published tree after that recipe merged: its pool is now exactly `['min_coverage=']` and **all three** keyword-swap mutations are caught, three rather than one because the old hole was substring-shaped.

The general form, and the sharpest version of this repository's most-repeated finding: **a check keyed on the presence of a string cannot distinguish a claim from an example of the claim being false.** Test files deliberately contain the strings describing exactly what they prove cannot happen — a trust-and-safety recipe's fixtures hold the attack strings it screens for, a citation guard's tests hold the forbidden spellings, a secrets scanner's tests hold things shaped like secrets. In each case presence means the opposite of what a naive audit concludes.

### Still open, filed separately

**#276** — the check enumerates polarity rather than deriving it, so `("x" in source) is False`, `count("x") == 0`, `len([…]) == 0` and an `IfExp` credit a spelling asserted **absent**; and the taint seed requires the literal `read_text`, so an `open()` read produces no taint. The under-match side matters as much: `all(…)`/`any(…)` pins are **refused**. No live instance across all 47 folders, and reachability was measured rather than assumed — `== False` is lint-blocked by E712, but `is False` is not, and `is False` is already house idiom in two recipes. It was filed rather than folded in on the reviewer's own reasoning: extending the ticket would make its title false about its contents, which was that round's subject.

### One operational finding worth the whole repository's attention

A reviewer's **successful** acquire of the single heavy-job lock happened while another agent still had **24 processes** running under its worktree. The previous holder had released the lock; releasing a lock file and finishing the work are two different events and nothing couples them. So the acquire was legitimate, the slot was free, and the machine was not. It released (ownership-checked), confirmed zero processes under any worktree, re-acquired, and ran alone — reporting that nothing it measured came from a contended window.

**A lock answers "may I start?", not "is the machine quiet?"** Those were the same question when one agent ran at a time and have not been since. Any figure depending on a quiet machine — a timing, a memory reading, a flaky-test verdict — must establish quiet separately from acquiring the right to cause it.

### What the recipe does

A five-way `Choice` classifying an *apparent* claim conflict as factual disagreement, time, entity, scope, or `not_conflicting` — the last being the honest answer for a false positive from whatever upstream detector flagged the pair. Python computes the temporal relationship and supplies it in the state; Jev reads it rather than deriving it.

### The finding that changed what this recipe teaches

Its builder reported a zero-request rule over the structured fields scoring 0.75 against Jev's 0.9375, with **the entire margin on the one category the rule structurally could not reach** — `entity` — because telling two same-named subjects apart "needs" reading the excerpts.

Its reviewer did not reason about that claim; it **built the rule**. **Every `entity` row's subject label was a bare two-word personal name, and no other row's was.** One regex fires on exactly the entity rows with **zero false positives across all 36**, and scores **1.0000** — beating Jev at zero requests. A second, independent route — comparing the two excerpts' appositive strings, using no label and no semantics — hits the identical rows and also scores 1.0000.

**It was not overfitting**, which is what made it decisive: the regex is derivable from the **three validation entity rows alone** and transfers to all sixteen test rows unchanged. The cause was in generation, not in balance — both entity excerpts in every row used the template `"<Name>, <role>, <claim>."` and no non-entity row did. **The author never wrote the label into a field; the template wrote it into the prose.**

The builder had come one step from finding this itself: a `pair_id` mutation produced the same perfect score and it **correctly dismissed that as illegitimate**, since fitting an identifier is cheating. **The step not taken was asking whether a *legitimate* feature does the same.** It does, twice. That is now a standing rule: whenever you rule a shortcut out of bounds, ask next whether something in bounds achieves the same result — dismissing a cheating feature closes only the cheating route, and it is precisely the moment you stop looking.

### How it was resolved, and why the recipe is stronger for it

**No fixture rebuild** — that was ruled against explicitly, since it would invalidate the whole evaluation for a narrower gain than disclosure. Instead the recipe now **ships the rival**: `name_pattern_baseline`, zero requests, scoring 1.0000 and **beating** the mechanism by 0.0625, pinned by counting in three tests proven live under mutation. Every necessity claim was rewritten to the true narrower one — a property of the chosen feature set, not of the task — across two docstrings, a fixture-builder comment, a renamed test, and three notebook locations including the committed cell output. The **cause** is named in both places a reader can meet it, with an explicit *"This is not evidence that reading excerpt text is unnecessary for entity diagnosis in general."*

So the recipe honestly reports a free hand-written rule outperforming the typed decision on its own fixture pool, and says why. Its reviewer ruled it **publishable and stronger than what it replaced**: the typed `Choice`, fixed option set, named fallback, Python-supplied temporal relationship, confidence gate, the mandated hard case and the adversarial injection are all intact, with the baseline comparison being one section rather than the recipe.

### A third round, for one word

The fix initially printed a `-0.0625` gap and then said the baseline **"ties"** Jev — in five places, including the committed output, a self-contradictory markdown sentence, and a test's own name. It blocked because a tie at equal or lower cost is *already* a loss, so calling a win a tie is one further step in the flattering direction, applied to the sentence carrying the verdict.

The evidence the reviewer used was a maintainer's own briefing message, which had said the recipe "reports, in its own committed output, that a zero-request rule **beats** the mechanism." It did not — it reported the gap and then said *ties*. **Someone who had read the diff closely, knew the finding, and was actively briefing its reviewer still supplied the correct conclusion the committed text withheld.** That is the mechanism of a softened scoreboard: it reads correctly to everyone who already knows the answer, which is everyone who wrote it and most who review it. The only reader it misleads is the one the artefact exists for.

The recorded test is to take the headline sentence **alone**, with no table above it, and ask what a reader concludes.

This is Level 4's first `Choice` + `Noul` combination, and it is the recipe the rule about counting quantities exists for: **22 input rows, 36 requests, 50 questions, 20 task-level units** — all four distinct, with questions exceeding requests because a Noul battery sends several propositions in one request. The composition boundary is part of the deliverable: stage one is always one request, stage two is a **later, conditional** one, and the notebook gates the fetch behind the condition rather than fetching and discarding.

### What the review process found, across four rounds

**Round 1 — the Noul half rested on a two-row template leak.** The recipe claimed a baseline could not reach the `entity`-style category because reading meaning was required. Its reviewer built the rule instead of reasoning about it: one proposition's positives shared a surface form no other row had, so a one-character feature separated the class with **zero false positives on validation** and transferred to test. The other proposition had **zero gold positives in validation**, no row where its tag determined an outcome, and no both-true row anywhere — so one of the two questions was never exercised in the positive direction on the split used to select its threshold.

**Round 2 — the fixtures were rebuilt**, with decoys added so cheap features had false positives available to hit, a validation positive added for the second proposition, and a row where that proposition's tag alone decides the outcome. The honest result moved **against** the mechanism, and the recipe said so.

**Round 3 — the leak survived, per proposition, and the probe was structurally blind to it.** This is the finding worth carrying furthest. The rebuilt probe honestly reported that no feature separated the **composed** flag — and a 223-feature sweep confirmed it. But the composed flag is an `any(...)` over two propositions, so the second proposition's positive **guarantees at least one false negative**, which means **a per-label leak can never reach perfect separation against a composed flag, by arithmetic rather than by luck.** Checked per proposition, one word reached 1.0 with zero false positives on both splits.

So the bar — zero false positives, reaching 1.0, transferring — is right, but **it is evaluated against a label, and the wrong label makes it unreachable.** Run the check at every granularity the recipe has a label for: per proposition in a battery, per option in a `Choice`, per rubric level in a `Score`, and then composed. The composed level is the **least** sensitive.

The recipe took the more informative resolution: rather than rewriting the leaky sentence, it **ships the rival as a named baseline** that beats the mechanism at zero requests, and its leak-check section now explains the arithmetic to a reader. A related correction landed in the same round: a probe reporting `fp=0` was a **dead** probe whose predicate never fired, so every probe now reports its **fire count** — a probe that never fires has not found nothing, it has measured nothing.

**Round 4 — one phrase.** The verdict sentence called stage two "a two-request semantic check" when it is one request carrying two propositions. On severity that was a sweep item: the error was *unflattering* and no figure moved. It was fixed anyway, because **it is the exact conflation this recipe was commissioned to make visible** — a recipe built to teach that distinction cannot ship with the distinction wrong in the sentence carrying its verdict, since it is what someone will cite when they get it right later.

### The honest result

On the eligible test rows the mechanism's raw tag **ties** two zero-request baselines and **loses** to a third. The recipe states it plainly — *"a tie goes to the cheaper baseline, so this is a loss for the mechanism, not a wash"* — names the condition under which the mechanism would earn its requests, and records that it gets that one case wrong, confidently. The sample is six rows and the recipe says so.

That is an unusual thing for a cookbook recipe to publish, and it is the right thing. The alternative was a margin that existed because the fixtures encoded the answer in their own prose.

## Recipe 49 (Multi-agent task assignment) merged — #285 as `b4e39ce`. **49 of 60 published; 37 merges**

A `Score` per (agent, subtask) pair, with a deterministic Python scheduler assigning work under capability, dependency and budget constraints Jev never sees. Rule-16's four quantities: **74 input rows, 74 requests, 74 questions, 12 task-level units** — task units **smaller** than requests, the inverse of the previous recipe where a Noul battery made questions exceed them.

### The constraint test, and the one thing a builder has not done before

The build notes asked for "a test shows constraints hold for any scores", which is where this project's most disguised failure lives: an earlier recipe proved a budget cap "whatever the model answers" on a 300-case fuzz where **0 of 300** iterations ever reached the cap, and deleting the guard under test left every advertised test green.

So the requirement was per-constraint binding counts, each asserted non-zero. This builder reported **capability 287/300, budget 294/300, and dependency 0/300** — and **it measured that zero rather than assuming it**, then built a **second dedicated scenario** where dependency binds, rather than softening the claim. That is the first time the counter has found a never-binding constraint here and the response was to add coverage.

Its reviewer then found the trap in the remedy: dependency binds 300/300 because it **cannot avoid** binding — one agent chases a two-agent pool a wave behind two siblings — so across 300 trials the scenario yields exactly **two** distinct outcomes. Not a fail-open, since the test's own comment says "true regardless of scores", but **"300 of 300" reads as 300 explorations when it is two**, and the recipe now says which.

### Three defects, all in committed prose or output

**A hand-typed count.** The cell computed `dependency_binds` — initialiser and increment both present — and **never read it**, printing a literal while the two counts beside it were interpolated, under a sentence claiming the counts were "printed as committed output, not only asserted in a test file". Nothing printed was false; a reviewer recomputed and got the same zero. **The defect is that the instrument could not report otherwise**, and the camouflage is mixed interpolation: a line presenting both halves with identical authority when only one is derived. Be most suspicious of a zero — it is the easiest literal to write and the hardest to doubt.

**A probe against the wrong label.** It tested whether a cue predicted *capability*, a structured fact, then concluded about *the gold ranking* through a step that does not follow. Its reviewer ran it properly — **975 features at 7 granularities** with fire counts — and found **no feature reaching zero false positives and perfect recall anywhere**, with even an oracle structured feature failing. So the conclusion was right and the evidence did not support it, which is a different defect from being wrong.

**And "wins outright on both splits" did not survive its own sweep.** The cue baseline *did* have a knob the cell said it lacked: sweeping 98 profile words finds one scoring **3/6 on validation at zero requests, tying the mechanism against 36 requests.** A tie at lower cost is a loss, so the verdict narrowed to **ties on validation, wins on test** — and the recipe now says *"the narrower claim is the one the cells above actually support."* Separately, the "capacity baseline" turned out to use **no capacity information at all**: every capacity and cost is 1, so it is **alphabetical order by agent id**, and the test margin is 4/6 against alphabetical's 3/6. It is now named accurately.

### A claim that was false, uncomputed, and plausibly the reviewer's own

The sweep cell asserted *"no word reaches 4/6 on test either."* One word did — reaching it only through **substring** matching, firing on an agent via "internal tools", while the cell's prose already described whole-word matching.

**The reviewer disclosed that the claim was probably its own.** Its first-round comment had said the same thing, and it **never measured it**: its reporting filters were top-ten-by-sum and `validation >= 3 AND test >= 4`, and the counterexample scores 1 on validation and 4 on test, so **it could not appear under either**. The claim was unfalsifiable by the instrument that produced it, and the builder reasonably wrote it down.

The fix took both halves — a word-boundary matcher and the claim **computed**: *"best test score reached by ANY of the 98 candidate words (whether or not validation would have selected it): 3/6, reached by 76 words."* That parenthetical names exactly the filter gap. And the reviewer then re-derived it by **writing the baseline itself from the cell's prose rather than lifting its code**, reporting the complete joint distribution because *"a ranked view is the instrument that failed me in round 1"* — finding **no `(·,4)` cell at all**, which is a stronger claim than any ranking could support.

**The general lesson, now recorded: a negative claim must be computed over the full space and reported as an extremum, not read off a ranked or thresholded view** — and a reviewer should hand a builder the *computation* rather than the conclusion, because a negative claim in a review comment becomes a committed sentence.
